key_terms.meaning: The default claim being tested, always written with an equality sign, e.g. H₀: μ = 50
The claim accepted when the sample evidence is too far from H₀; it may be one-sided (μ > 50) or two-sided (μ ≠ 50)
Rejecting H₀ when it is true; probability α, called the level of significance
Accepting H₀ when it is false; probability β
Probability of correctly rejecting a false H₀; power = 1 − β
The largest chance of a false alarm the tester is willing to allow, usually 0.05 or 0.01
The set of test-statistic values for which H₀ is rejected; its boundary is the critical value
The probability, computed under H₀, of a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed; reject H₀ if p ≤ α
A sample quantity with a known distribution under H₀, used to make the decision, e.g. z = (x̄ − μ₀)/(σ/√n)

key_terms.term: Large sample z-test for a mean
key_terms.meaning: For n ≥ 30, z = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n) is roughly N(0,1) by the central limit theorem
z = (x̄₁ − x̄₂)/√(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂) tests H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ for large independent samples
z = (p̂ − p₀)/√(p₀(1 − p₀)/n), used when np₀ and n(1 − p₀) both exceed 5
t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n) when σ is unknown and n is small; it follows t with ν = n − 1 degrees of freedom
The number of independent pieces of information left after estimating parameters; for one sample, ν = n − 1
Test on differences of matched pairs, t = d̄/(s_d/√n) with ν = n − 1 pairs
F = s₁²/s₂², the ratio of two independent sample variances from normal populations; follows F with (n₁ − 1, n₂ − 1) degrees of freedom under H₀: σ₁² = σ₂²
χ² = Σ (Oᵢ − Eᵢ)²/Eᵢ, the sum of squared standardized differences between observed and expected counts
Chi-square test of whether observed frequencies match a claimed distribution; ν = k − 1 − m, where m is the number of estimated parameters
Chi-square test on an r × c contingency table with expected count E = (row total × column total)/grand total and ν = (r − 1)(c − 1)
F = MSB/MSW = between-group mean square ÷ within-group mean square; large F means the group means differ
One-way classifies data by a single factor; two-way also blocks out a second factor (and its interaction) to reduce error

takeaways: A hypothesis test asks whether sample data are too far from what H₀ predicts, with the allowed false-alarm rate fixed in advance as α.
Type I and Type II errors pull in opposite directions: lowering α for a fixed sample size raises β, so the only way to shrink both is a larger sample.
The p-value is evidence against H₀ on a continuous scale; α is the decision line fixed before the data are seen.
For n ≥ 30 the central limit theorem lets you use z even when σ is unknown and replaced by s.
When n is small and σ is unknown, s fluctuates a lot, so the correct reference curve is Student's t with n − 1 degrees of freedom, which has heavier tails than the normal.
The F test compares two variances as a ratio; the ratio is close to 1 when the population variances are equal.
Chi-square tests work on counts, not on measured values, and need every expected count to be at least about 5.
ANOVA compares several means at once by splitting total variation into between-group and within-group parts, then taking an F ratio of the two mean squares.
bank_note: Long answers here are marked on four steps: state the assumptions, write the test statistic with its distribution and degrees of freedom, compute against the correct table value, and end with a conclusion written in the words of the original problem, with the ANOVA or chi-square table shown in full.

bank.q: Define null and alternative hypotheses. Explain Type I and Type II errors with a decision table, and show how α, β and the power of a test are related.
outline: H₀ is the maintained claim with an equality; H₁ is what the test is trying to establish
2×2 table: true state (H₀ true / H₀ false) against decision (reject / do not reject)
Type I = reject a true H₀, probability α; Type II = fail to reject a false H₀, probability β
Power = 1 − β; increasing sample size lowers β for the same α
Numerical illustration: a medicine tested for side effects

bank.q: Explain level of significance, critical region and p-value, and describe the general procedure of a hypothesis test.
outline: Fix H₀ and H₁ before seeing data; choose α
Choose a test statistic whose distribution under H₀ is known
Critical region from the tables; state the decision rule
p-value = probability of a result at least as extreme as observed, under H₀
Reject H₀ if p ≤ α; p is not the probability that H₀ is true

bank.q: Explain the chi-square distribution, its properties and its uses in testing. Describe the procedure of the chi-square goodness of fit test.
outline: χ² with ν degrees of freedom is the sum of squares of ν independent standard normals; mean ν, variance 2ν; skewed, defined for positive values
Conditions: counts, not measurements; independent observations; every expected count ≥ 5
Statistic χ² = Σ (Oᵢ − Eᵢ)²/Eᵢ
Degrees of freedom k − 1 − m when m parameters are estimated from the data
Conclusion stated in words of the problem

bank.q: Describe one-way analysis of variance: assumptions, the partition of total sum of squares, the ANOVA table and the decision rule.
outline: Assumptions: independent samples, normal populations, equal variances
SST = SSB + SSW with degrees of freedom k − 1, N − k, N − 1
Mean squares MSB = SSB/(k − 1) and MSW = SSW/(N − k)
F = MSB/MSW with (k − 1, N − k) degrees of freedom
Reject equality of means when F exceeds the table value

bank.q: A sample of 100 bulbs shows a mean life of 1200 hours with a standard deviation of 100 hours. Test at the 5% level the claim that the population mean life is 1250 hours.
outline: H₀: μ = 1250, H₁: μ ≠ 1250 (two-tailed)
Critical values ±1.96 at α = 0.05
|z| = 5 > 1.96, so reject H₀
p-value is far below 0.05; the claim is not supported

bank.q: In two large cities, 400 of 1000 sampled users in city A and 450 of 1200 in city B use a payment app. Test whether the two proportions differ at the 1% level.
outline: H₀: p₁ = p₂ against H₁: p₁ ≠ p₂
z = (0.40 − 0.375)/SE, compare with ±2.58
Check that the samples are large and independent

bank.q: A sample of 10 packets from a filling machine gives a mean weight of 495 g and a sample standard deviation of 8 g. Test at the 5% level whether the average fill is below the stated 500 g.
outline: σ unknown and n small, so use Student's t
H₀: μ = 500, H₁: μ < 500 (one-tailed)
Table value t₀.₀₅, ₉ = 1.833, so reject H₀
State the assumption of a normal population

bank.q: Two machines produce rods whose lengths are measured on 10 rods each. Explain, with a worked calculation, how the paired t-test differs from the two-sample t-test and when each is used.
outline: Paired design: same item measured twice, so test the differences d
t = d̄/(s_d/√n) with n − 1 degrees of freedom on the differences
Independent samples: pooled variance s_p², degrees of freedom n₁ + n₂ − 2
Why pairing removes item-to-item variation
Choice of design follows how the data were collected, not the arithmetic

bank.q: Two samples of sizes 10 and 12 from normal populations give variances 24 and 9. Test at the 5% level whether the population variances are equal.
outline: H₀: σ₁² = σ₂², H₁: σ₁² ≠ σ₂²
F = s₁²/s₂² = 24/9 = 2.67 with (9, 11) degrees of freedom
Two-tailed test: compare with F₀.₀₂₅(9, 11) and the reciprocal lower tail
Conclude whether the ratio is significant
Note the F test is sensitive to non-normality

bank.q: A die is thrown 120 times and the six faces appear 15, 22, 25, 18, 20 and 20 times. Test at the 5% level whether the die is fair.
outline: H₀: the die is fair, so each expected count is 20
χ² = Σ (O − E)²/E = 3.0
ν = 6 − 1 = 5 (no parameter estimated)
Table value χ²₀.₀₅, ₅ = 11.07; 3.0 < 11.07, do not reject
Conclude the deviations are consistent with chance

bank.q: A survey cross-classifies 200 people by gender and by preference for three schemes. Show how to set up the chi-square test of independence and compute the degrees of freedom.
outline: H₀: the two attributes are independent
Expected count = (row total × column total)/grand total
Sum (O − E)²/E over all cells
ν = (r − 1)(c − 1); for 2 × 3 this is 2
Every expected count should be at least 5, else merge categories
Reject independence if χ² exceeds the table value

bank.q: Compare the z-test, Student's t-test, F-test and chi-square test: the question each answers, the assumptions each needs, and how they are connected.
outline: z: means or proportions, large sample or known σ, normal reference curve
t: means, σ unknown, small sample, heavier tails than normal
F: ratio of two variances; also the test for equality of several means in ANOVA
For two groups, t² equals the ANOVA F — the same information, different bookkeeping
Chi-square: counts and variances of normal samples; squared standard normal is χ²₁
Choosing wrongly (e.g. t when σ is known) costs power or validity

bank.q: A supplier claims a mean strength of 50 MPa. Explain step by step how you would set up and carry out the test, how you would choose between a z and a t procedure, and how the consequences of Type I and Type II errors affect the choice of α.
outline: Write H₀ and H₁ in the units of the problem; decide one- or two-sided from the claim
Check sample size and whether σ is known; pick z or t and its degrees of freedom
Fix α according to which error is more costly (safety versus cost of rejection)
Compute the statistic, the p-value and the decision
Report the conclusion in words plus a confidence interval for the mean
Remark that a non-significant result is not evidence that H₀ is exactly true

bank.q: Why is analysis of variance preferred to running separate t-tests on every pair of means? Explain the error-rate problem and the role of the within-group variance.
outline: k groups give k(k − 1)/2 pairwise tests; each at α, the chance of at least one false alarm grows
ANOVA tests all means equal in one test at a fixed α
MSW is the pooled estimate of the common σ² and sets the yardstick
F = MSB/MSW; a large ratio means group means are spread more than chance allows
If only some pairs differ, follow-up multiple-comparison procedures are needed

glossary.def: A statement about a population parameter that is either true or false but is tested using sample data.
A hypothesis that fixes the parameter completely, such as H₀: μ = 50.
A hypothesis that allows a range of values, such as H₁: μ > 50.
A test where the critical region lies entirely in one tail, used for directional alternatives.
A test where the critical region is split between both tails, used for alternatives of the form μ ≠ μ₀.
The boundary value of the test statistic that separates the acceptance and rejection regions at a given α.
The set of test-statistic values for which H₀ is not rejected.
A test in which a statistic is compared with its standard error to judge whether a difference could be due to chance.
The standard deviation of the sampling distribution of a statistic, such as σ/√n for a sample mean.
For large n, the sample mean is approximately normally distributed whatever the shape of the population.
A test whose power tends to 1 as the sample size grows.
A symmetric bell-shaped distribution with heavier tails than the normal, indexed by degrees of freedom; arises when σ is estimated by s.
The count of independent deviations available after the sample has been used to estimate parameters.
A combined estimate of a common variance, s_p² = [(n₁ − 1)s₁² + (n₂ − 1)s₂²]/(n₁ + n₂ − 2).
The distribution of the ratio of two independent chi-square variables each divided by its degrees of freedom; used for variance ratios.
The distribution of a sum of squares of independent standard normal variables; skewed right, with mean equal to its degrees of freedom.
The count actually recorded in a category or cell of a table.
The count predicted for a category under H₀, for example npᵢ or (row total × column total)/grand total.
A two-way table of counts classifying items by two attributes.
A continuity correction applied to the chi-square test in a 2 × 2 table to reduce overestimation of significance.
The categorical variable whose levels define the groups in an ANOVA.
Variation of observations about their own group mean; it measures the background noise.
Variation of group means about the overall mean; it grows when the group means really differ.
A follow-up procedure that compares individual pairs of means while holding the overall error rate fixed.
